A 62-year-old woman with a history of metabolic syndrome presented with chest pain persisting for four months, without any increase in frequency or duration. She reported no pain at rest, nocturnal pain, difficulty breathing, or palpitations. An echocardiographic stress examination indicated significant ischemia with anteroseptal hypokinesia, while cardiac chambers appeared morphologically normal. Coronary angiography identified stenosis in the proximal left anterior descending coronary artery (LAD) near the left main stem. A stent was placed in the proximal LAD, resulting in no residual stenosis. The ventricle was morphologically normal. Follow-up coronary angiography 13 months post-stent implantation showed no re-stenosis and a normal left ventricle. No echocardiogram was conducted at this follow-up.

A transthoracic echocardiography disclosed a big (70 × 30 mm) mass in the left atrium attached to the interatrial septum. The tumor prolapsed into the left ventricle obstructing the mitral valve orifice. The mean pressure gradient across the mitral valve was 8 mm Hg.

A 14-year-old boy presented with multiple white, non-itchy areas on his distal extremities for two years. The lesions included whitish papules and depressed areas with central protrusion. On clinical examination, the patient, who appeared otherwise healthy, exhibited lumbar lordosis, laxity in large joints, tibia vara, high-arched palate, and dental misalignment. The skin lesions were scattered, white to skin-colored papules, less than 1 centimeter in diameter, with central protrusion, located on the dorsum of fingers, forearms, distal portion of the thighs, and calves. No lesions were found on the trunk or proximal areas of the extremities. Palms, soles, dorsum of feet, and mucosal membranes were unaffected. There were no sensory changes associated with the lesions. The patient had no history of medication use. Family history was negative. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, urinalysis, and blood chemistry (erythrocyte sedimentation rate and liver function tests), were within normal limits. Antinuclear antibody was negative. The patient had no risk factors for AIDS or syphilis, so HIV and VDRL tests were not requested. Hepatitis B surface antigens were not detected. Immunological assays for IgM, IgA, IgG, IgE, C3, and C4 levels were normal. A 0.5 centimeter induration was observed after tuberculin testing. Chest x-ray was normal.

Haematoxylin and eosin stained section showed faintly eosinophilic separated collagen fibers in the upper and mid-dermis. Verhoeff-vanGieson stained sections showed a marked decrease or in some areas total absence of elastic fibres, in both superficial and mid-dermis. Elastic fibres around the vessels in the affected areas are also fragmented and markedly decreased.

A 43-year-old woman with a long-standing history of schizophrenia since 1982, and previous hospitalization aimed at improving social communication skills at the age of 23, reported experiencing mild pain in her left flank and back. In 1995, she underwent ureterolysis and ureteroureterostomy due to left-sided ureteral obstruction. Histological examination of the biopsy showed benign fibrous tissue proliferations. No additional evaluation or surgical removal was planned at that time due to her deteriorating mental condition. She was placed under regular follow-up with imaging studies. In May 2002, she was referred from the psychiatric hospital to the Department of Urology as the mass exhibited growth.

CT scan with contrast enhancement revealed a tumor located between iliocostalis and psoas muscles in retroperitoneal space. The peripheral part of the tumor was enhanced, while the central part did not. The left paravertebral muscles around the tumor showed atrophy. The medial margin of the tumor was deformed by a left transverse process of the second lumber spine. Coronal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated the tumor to be located beneath the left kidney. The central part of the tumor was found to be of iso/low intensity in the T1-weighted phase and of heterogeneously high intensity in the T2-weighted phase. The marginal part showed very low intensity in both phases. Needle biopsy revealed that the tumor consisted of well-proliferated spindle cells rich in collagen fibers.

Three years following a cubital procaine-HCL 0.05% injection that resulted in acute severe local pain radiating to his forearm and wrist, a 33-year-old man reported pain in his right hand. Two months later, he experienced numbness in the area served by the right median nerve and observed wasting of the thenar muscles. Additionally, there was noticeable muscular atrophy in his right forearm. Nerve conduction studies revealed an increased distal latency in the median nerve, a very low thenar compound muscle action potential upon median nerve stimulation, a reduced sensory conduction velocity of 39 m/s in the median nerve upon thumb stimulation, and no sensory nerve action potential upon stimulation of the 2nd and 3rd fingers. Electromyography of the right biceps brachii muscle was normal. In the right abductor pollicis brevis muscle, there were fibrillations, increased duration and amplitude of motor unit potentials, and a reduced recruitment pattern. Forearm muscles were not examined. Surgical intervention was performed for carpal tunnel syndrome. Ten months later, the patient was admitted to our department due to the persistence of his symptoms.

Nerve conduction studies showed an increased distal latency in the median nerve, a very low thenar compound muscle action potential on median nerve stimulation, a reduced sensory conduction velocity of 39 m/s in the median nerve on thumb stimulation and no sensory nerve action potential on stimulation of the 2nd and 3rd fingers. Electromyography of the right biceps brachii muscle was normal. In the fibrillations, an increased duration and amplitude of motor unit potentials and reduced recruitment pattern were found in the right abductor pollicis brevis muscle. Nerve conduction studies showed no response over the thenar muscle on median nerve stimulation at the wrist and elbow. Fibrillations and sparse motor unit potentials with increased duration and amplitude (up to 10 mV) were found in flexor digitorum superficialis muscle, in contrast to the normal Electromyography-findings of the right flexor carpi ulnaris. On median nerve stimulation at the elbow a low compound muscle action potential with an increased distal latency was recorded over flexor digitorum superficialis muscle in the right side (right: amplitude 1 mV, latency 9.0 ms, left: amplitude 7 mV, latency 3.2 ms). No sensory nerve action potential was recorded at the wrist on stimulation of the 1st, 2nd or 3rd finger. Somatosensory evoked potentials of the left median and right radial and ulnar nerve were normal. No potential was recorded at Erb's point in the supraclavicular fossa, at the sixth and second cervical vertebra and the contralateral cortex on median nerve stimulation on the right. Palpation along the median nerve revealed a fusiform mass at the distal third of the right upper arm, which could be confirmed by MRI. Histological investigation revealed marked peri- and endoneurial fibrosis, severe axonal loss as well as proliferation of concentric whorl-like formations resulting in multicompartment arrangement. These pseudo onion-bulb formations showed strong immunoreactivity for the epithelial membrane antigen and were predominantly negative for S-100 protein. In addition, small groups of regenerating axonal sprouts surrounded by perineurial ensheathment were visible.

He stayed there for 24 hours before being moved to the Internal Medicine Ward. Additionally, he received chloroquine 150 mg daily starting from 24th April 2001. He was discharged on 19th May 2001. On 6th June 2001, he was readmitted with a febrile syndrome.

A 75-year-old male with diabetes reported experiencing dull pain in the upper abdomen for one week and observed swelling in the left upper abdomen. He did not have vomiting, fever, or gastrointestinal bleeding. His medical and family history were unremarkable, and he did not smoke or consume alcohol. Physical examination revealed a 14 × 10 cm mass in the epigastrium and left hypochondrium with minimal intrinsic mobility. Routine biochemical tests were normal. Imaging studies, including an ultrasonogram and CT scan of the abdomen, identified a large heterogeneous mass measuring 13 × 10 cm, extending from the tail of the pancreas to the anterior pararenal space, lesser sac, and gastrosplenic ligament, enveloping the posterior aspect of the fundus, body, and greater curvature of the stomach. One day post-admission, the palpable mass size reduced to 8 × 6 cm without worsening symptoms. A repeat ultrasonography showed the mass size decreased to 8 × 8 cm. Upper endoscopy revealed a large bulge in the fundus and corpus of the stomach posteriorly, with an opening in the posterior part of the corpus, edematous margins, and the release of serous fluid and necrotic material into the stomach. Fluid analysis was normal for CEA and CA 19-9.

Biopsy taken from the edge of the opening showed bundles of spindle cells with elongated nuclei and tumor cells and was strongly positive for CD117 immunohistochemical examination.

A 31-year-old man presented with a painless tumor in the left inguinal region, which had gradually increased in size over the past six months. On physical examination, a subcutaneous tumor the size of a fist was noted in the inguinal area. The skin over the tumor appeared normal without any ulceration, and there was no enlargement of the inguinal lymph nodes. Computed tomography showed a solid tumor with heterogeneous contrast enhancement located in the adipose tissue, with no evidence of metastases to the liver or lungs. A wide local excision with a resection margin of at least 20 mm was performed. The excised tumor measured 124 × 105 mm, was solid, encapsulated, and had a homogeneous yellowish-white appearance without central necrosis or hemorrhage on its cut surface. Routine histological examination using hematoxylin-and-eosin staining revealed spindle-shaped cells with high cellularity in some areas and two mitoses per 10 high-power fields.

The tumor cells showed only immunoreactivity for desmin and alpha-smooth muscle actin.

A 5-year-old male was admitted to Children Medical Center (CMC) with inflammation and swelling in his left mandible and wrist, with no history of trauma. He had a history of multiple pneumonia episodes starting at seven months old. Upon admission, laboratory results showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 84 mm/h, a white blood cell (WBC) count of 12100/mm3 (61% neutrophils, 39% lymphocytes), hemoglobin level of 11.3 g/dl, and a thrombocyte count of 386000/mm3. C-reactive protein (CRP) was 20 mg/dl, leading to the initiation of cephalexin (150 mg/kg/day). Radiographic imaging revealed osteolytic lesions in the distal metaphase of the hand and maxillary bone. Given his history of recurrent infections and multifocal osteomyelitis, a bone biopsy was performed, and immune system function was assessed. The bone biopsy showed non-necrotizing granulomatoid lesions. The purified protein derivative reaction had an induration of 10 mm. Tests for HIV, hepatitis B surface antigen (HBs), rheumatoid factor, and brucella agglutination were negative. Serum IgG was 1650 mg/dl (normal: 441–1135 mg/dl), with IgM and IgA in the high normal range at 250 and 175 mg/dl, respectively. No defects were found in humoral and cellular immunity, so phagocytic cell function was tested using a nitroblue-tetrazolium (NBT) slide test. Based on hematological and immunological tests (NBT = 0), antibiotic therapy was changed from cephalexin to co-trimoxazole (20 mg/kg/day, iv) along with interferon-γ (50 microgram/m2 every other day). After two weeks of treatment, the patient's condition improved, and he was discharged with a prescription for oral cephalexin (100 mg/kg/day) and co-trimoxazole (10 mg/kg/day) as prophylaxis. Eight months later, the patient was readmitted with a tender mass in the right upper quadrant (RUQ), severe dyspnea, persistent cough, and chest and abdominal pain in the epigastric area that had started 10 days prior. He was placed on cephalexin (100 mg/kg/day). A computerized tomography (CT) scan of the chest and abdomen revealed a hypodense area in the liver, with adjacent involvement of the lower right ribs and soft tissue reaction, indicating rib osteomyelitis. Sonography-guided drainage of the hepatic abscess was performed, and a sample was sent to the Mycology Department at Tehran University of Medical Sciences.

The microscopic examination of clarified specimen with KOH 10% indicated the branched, septated and dichotomous mycelia. The remaining specimen was also cultured on Brain Heart Infusion agar (BHI), Sabouraud's dextrose agar (S) and Sabouraud's containing 0.005% chloramphenicol (Sc). The S and Sc culture media were incubated at 25°C and BHI at 37°C. The colonies grew rapidly, attaining the diameter of 5 cm within 5 days and their color was bluish green. Cellophane tape preparations and slide cultures demonstrated septated, branched and hyaline hyphae with rough-walled conidiophores and radiated conidial heads.

An 82-year-old man was admitted to the hospital presenting with melaena and dizziness upon standing. His medical history included systemic sclerosis diagnosed three years prior and pulmonary fibrosis. He was on prednisolone and azathioprine. There was no history of liver disease or alcohol abuse. On physical examination, his blood pressure was 95/65 mmHg, and his pulse was 90 beats per minute. Bilateral fine inspiratory crackles were noted. The abdomen was soft and non-tender. Rectal examination confirmed melaena. Laboratory results showed a white blood cell count of 12,700/mm3, haemoglobin level of 10.9 g/dl, platelet count of 186,000/mm3, and mean corpuscular volume of 99.4 fl. Blood urea was 12.5 mmol/l, creatinine 68 μmol/l, with normal electrolytes and glucose at 6.3 mmol/l. Liver function tests revealed serum alanine aminotransferase at 12 u/l, bilirubin at 12 μmol/l, γ-glutamyl transferase at 54 u/l, alkaline phosphatase at 35 u/l, total protein at 52 g/l, albumin at 27 g/l, and C-reactive protein at 12. Coagulation studies were within normal limits. Factor V Leiden mutation was absent. Hepatitis viral serology and autoantibody screen were negative, and α-1-antitrypsin levels were normal. Ferritin was 103 μmol/l, caeruloplasmin was 0.25 μmol/l, and α-fetoprotein was 0.9 kU/L. Urgent gastroscopy identified oesophageal varices, fresh blood, and clots in the stomach. During the procedure, the oesophageal varices began to bleed. Haemostasis was not achieved with sclerotherapy, necessitating the insertion of a Sengstaken tube. The patient was admitted to the High Dependency Unit, started on intravenous glypressin and antibiotics, and received a transfusion of four units of blood. A repeat gastroscopy the following day showed two columns of grade II oesophageal varices, two oesophageal ulcers likely secondary to sclerotherapy, and mild portal gastropathy.

There was no evidence of any excess inflammation and no features to suggest cirrhosis or drug-induced liver disease. Overall this was essentially normal liver tissue. Ultrasound scan of the abdomen revealed a small liver with coarse texture and no focal lesion. Hepato-portal flow was demonstrated in the portal vein. The common bile duct was of normal caliber. The spleen was enlarged (bipolar length 12.8 cm). A moderate amount of free peritoneal fluid was noted. CT scan confirmed the absence of portal vein thrombosis.

A 41-year-old female with a history of NF1 presented with a 3-year history of recurrent epigastric soreness, heartburn, and diarrhea. Endoscopic examinations repeatedly showed recurrent duodenal ulcers. Symptoms were alleviated with proton-pump inhibitors but returned upon cessation of the medication. The patient had a family history of NF1, with her brother, sister, and second son also exhibiting fully developed features of the condition. She exhibited normal intellectual development without cognitive dysfunction or learning disabilities. Physical examination identified several café-au-lait spots, multiple small nodules on the anterior chest and areolar area, and multiple axillary freckles. A biopsy of a skin nodule confirmed neurofibromas. During admission, upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed multiple shallow ulcers in the descending duodenum. Tests for Helicobacter pylori, including the rapid urease test and urea breath test, were negative.

The serum fasting gastrin level was >1,000 pg/mL and 837 pg/mL in two consecutive measurements. Abdominal computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans showed a 3 × 2-cm, clearly defined, well-enhanced mass adjacent to the duodenal loop in the subhepatic space. No metastatic lesions were observed in the liver or regional lymph nodes.

There was no history of tobacco, alcohol, illicit substance, or medication use during the pregnancy. A routine prenatal ultrasound identified a cardiac echogenic focus and a potential anatomical heart defect, leading to the child's transfer to the neonatal intensive care unit at birth. A thoracic echocardiogram revealed mitral stenosis, aortic stenosis, and coarctation of the aorta. Surgical intervention was performed to repair the coarctation, and a right diaphragmatic eventration was also corrected during the same procedure. No cardiac arrhythmias were detected on telemetry during the initial hospitalization.

On initial physical examination, his temperature was 38°C, and he had multiple pseudofolliculitis, as well as oral and scrotal ulcerations. Laboratory tests on admission showed a haemoglobin level of 13 g/dl, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 105 mm/hr, and a C-reactive protein concentration of 204 mg/l. A 23-year-old male was referred by his general dental practitioner. One year prior, an x-ray revealed a cyst associated with an ectopic lower right canine tooth. The patient had an uneventful medical history and no notable intraoral clinical findings, except for the absence of tooth 43. Radiographic examination showed a 3 cm unicystic radiolucent area with clear boundaries. Tooth 43 was situated at the base of this area. There was no evidence of root apex resorption. The lesion was surgically removed under general anesthesia and the cavity was filled with pelvic spongiosa. The separation of the lesion from the mandibular bone was uncomplicated. The postoperative recovery was uneventful.

The tumor is solid and there is a cyst formation. The epithelium is in the form of whorled masses of spindle cells as well as sheets and plexiform strands. Rings of columnar cells give rise to duct-like appearance. Calcification is sometimes seen and may be extensive.

A 69-year-old woman presented 11 years ago with intermittent mild to moderate pain on the right side of her abdomen, described as a dull ache, accompanied by nausea, bloating, and flatulence. She also experienced constipation, with partial symptom relief following defecation. Symptoms worsened after heavy meals, and she occasionally had steatorrhea. Physical examination showed mild right-sided abdominal tenderness. She had no other health issues and no history of abdominal surgery. Initial investigations, including an abdominal ultrasound scan (USS), a hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid (HIDA) scan, and an oesophago-gastro-duodenoscopy (OGD), showed no abnormalities. Flexible sigmoidoscopy and colonoscopy were also unremarkable. She was advised to take laxatives regularly, which provided partial and temporary relief. Her symptoms persisted, and almost two years later, she underwent an endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP), a cream absorption test, a wheat intolerance test, and a CT scan of her abdomen, all of which were normal. She was advised to take antispasmodics, various combinations of laxatives, and a course of Pancrelipase (Creon) tablets, which provided only temporary relief. A gastroenterology consultant recommended another abdominal USS, OGD, and a barium follow-through study, all of which were normal. She continued to receive symptomatic treatment.

Histopathological analysis revealed a densely crowded spindle and polygonal cell tumour showing moderate nuclear pleomorphism. No mitoses were found and the tumour spread into the mucosa and outwards into the serosa. There was no lymph nodal spread. A 74-year-old female with a history of severe aortic stenosis and interventricular septal hypertrophy underwent bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement along with septal myectomy. Two months after the surgery, she experienced syncope and was admitted to another hospital. At presentation, the patient, who is obese, had a heart rate of 40 beats per minute and stable blood pressure. There was no jugular venous distention, but occasional cannon A waves were observed. Lung examination showed adequate aeration in all fields without crackles or wheezing. The point of maximum impulse was not displaced. Heart sounds were regular with variable intensity, without atrial or ventricular gallops, but an early systolic murmur grade II/VI was noted at the left sternal border. Due to symptomatic bradycardia, a dual chamber pacemaker was recommended and successfully implanted. The patient was discharged 24 hours after the procedure. Four months later, during a follow-up visit, she reported no complaints and was doing well. An echocardiogram showed normal left ventricular systolic function and proper functioning of the prosthetic aortic valve, with no other abnormalities.

An echocardiogram obtained at the time of her initial visit, while still asymptomatic, showed normal left ventricular chamber dimensions, systolic function, and bioprosthetic valve function. In addition, a pacer wire that was correctly positioned in the right ventricular apex was also seen. However, an abnormal color flow signal arising from the interventricular septum with a predominant flow away from the transducer into the left ventricular cavity was noted. Continuous and pulse wave Doppler interrogation demonstrated a continuous flow with a predominant diastolic component. This abnormal color flow signal, traversing the interventricular septum, was never identified in previous studies.

A 34-year-old woman reported experiencing intermittent lower abdominal pain and abdominal distension for five months. She did not have any gastrointestinal bleeding, nausea, vomiting, or changes in bowel habits. There was no history of seizures, cognitive issues, behavioral problems, or skin abnormalities. She had a caesarean section seven months prior. Physical examination revealed a midline reducible incisional hernia with minimal tenderness in the right iliac fossa. A computed tomography scan showed an unexplained density in the right iliac fossa, potentially related to the caecum or pericaecal area. An infraumbilical incisional hernia containing bowel loops was also observed. Colonoscopy revealed erythema at the ileo-caecal junction, but biopsies from this area were normal. Magnetic resonance imaging confirmed a mass in the right iliac fossa, separate from and lying inferior to the caecum. Both ovaries appeared normal. During surgery, a retroperitoneal mass was found and excised, and the hernia was repaired. The mass was well-circumscribed with a thin fibrous capsule and had a soft consistency. The cut surface displayed lobules of fatty tissue interspersed with bands and nodules of firm white tissue with a whorled appearance.

Microscopic examination showed a lesion composed of lobules of mature fatty tissue harbouring multiple variable sized nodules of smooth muscle fibres. The smooth muscle fibres were arranged in broad interlacing fascicles. No cytological atypia was seen and only one mitotic figure was identified in the multiple sections examined and no necrosis. No proliferation of medium-sized arteries with thick muscular walls was observed. The spindle cells were positive for smooth muscle actin and desmin and negative for CD34 and CD117. The staining for HMB-45 was not performed, as blocks were not available.

In 1993 and 1997, she had benign colonic polyps which were excised endoscopically. In March and June 2003, she was referred to our surgical outpatient department with subcutaneous lesions, first on the left side of the abdominal wall and then on the right buttock.

The lesions were excised under local anesthesia and were reported to be sebaceous adenomas.

A 60-year-old woman presented with a painful nodule in the left lobe of the thyroid. She had no history of head and neck radiation and no family history of thyroid or parathyroid conditions. The nodule had not significantly changed in size, but the pain persisted and was exacerbated by talking. She did not experience any changes in her voice. Five years prior, she had been evaluated for pain radiating over the left side of her face, at which time a small, firm nodule in the left thyroid lobe was detected. A needle biopsy at that time showed no signs of malignancy, and the condition was identified as a benign nodular goiter, with observation recommended. An ultrasound revealed a mass in the left lower thyroid lobe measuring 2.7 × 1.6 × 2.7 cm, containing both cystic and solid components. Her serum ionized calcium level was within normal limits, but her intact parathyroid hormone (PTH) level was elevated to three times the upper limit of normal. Due to ongoing facial pain, a left thyroid lobectomy and isthmusectomy were performed. During surgery, a firm, multinodular left thyroid lobe was observed. No abnormal central compartment lymph nodes were identified or removed.

Pathological examination of the specimen revealed a large, yellowish tumor measuring 2.7 × 2.0 × 2.0 cm that was pushing into the left thyroid lobe, but separated from it by a fibrous capsule. The mass was noted to be composed of monomorphous parathyroid cells without significant necrosis or mitotic activity. There was invasion into the thyroid capsule and into adjacent fatty tissue. No vascular invasion was noted. Further immunohistochemical studies found the tumour did not express: Thyroid Transcription Factor – 1, Calcitonin, and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), but did express Chromagranin, Synaptophysin, Bcl -2 and Cytokeratin 7.

A 25-year-old male presented with a history of cough producing bloody mucoid sputum for the past two months. He also experienced anorexia and had a history of intermittent upper respiratory tract infections over the last two years. Physical examination revealed reduced breath sounds at the right lung base. Laboratory tests showed normochromic-normocytic anemia, low serum iron levels, and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (76 mm/first hour). A chest radiograph indicated a peripheral opacity in the right lung, and a computed tomography (CT) scan revealed a soft tissue density mass in the right lower lobe. No enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes were observed. Bronchoscopy results were negative. Transthoracic fine-needle aspiration under CT guidance did not yield diagnostic results. Comprehensive imaging of the bone, brain, and abdomen showed no extrapulmonary involvement. Surgical intervention was performed for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes. The patient underwent a right lower lobectomy and complete lymph node dissection via a right posterolateral thoracotomy. The mass was well-circumscribed and yellowish in color on macroscopic examination.

Microscopically the mass was composed of fibroblasts, collagen and inflammatory cells mainly of lymphocytes and plasma cells. There was no mitotic activity. No microorganisms were detected even on special stains.

A 21-year-old patient from Sudan, socially identified as female, was referred for evaluation due to delayed puberty. The patient was assigned female at birth by a midwife and raised accordingly. The patient identifies as female and was hesitant to discuss sexual attraction, possibly due to cultural reasons. Physical examination revealed the patient was dressed in female attire, had no facial hair, displayed muscular build, broad shoulders, wide nipple spacing, and lacked breast development. The patient measured approximately 175 cm in height and had a female voice. Examination of the external genitalia showed Type IV FGM, with no pubic hair or increased pigmentation in the genital area. A rectal examination suggested the presence of a prostate. Hormonal analysis showed a serum prolactin level of 215 Mu/L, FSH of 0.5 Mu/L, and LH of 1.1 Mu/L (normal ranges: serum prolactin: 60–370 Mu/L, serum FSH: 1–8 Mu/L, serum LH: 2–10 Mu/L).

Cytogenetic analysis showed a normal male karyotype, 46, XY. Ultrasound examination confirmed the presence of a 15 × 15 mm diameter soft tissue mass in the position of the male prostate.

A 53-year-old male from Mexico presented to the San Francisco General Hospital chest clinic with a history of chronic cough and pulmonary nodules. His respiratory symptoms began in 1985 with an intermittent cough that gradually became chronic and productive of yellow sputum, accompanied by mild shortness of breath. In 1997, he was treated with inhaled bronchodilators in Mexico with minimal relief. After immigrating to the United States in 2004, he was treated with a steroid inhaler by a primary care provider, also without relief. A chest radiograph was performed, leading to his referral to the chest clinic. During his visit, he reported no current fevers, chills, sweats, weight loss, eye pain, joint pain, rash, or sinusitis. He had no pets, mold exposure, recent travel, or environmental tobacco smoke exposure. He reported no other medical conditions and denied tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drug use. His occupational history included working at a charcoal production plant in Mexico from ages 18 to 26, where he spent 10-12 hours a day burning wood to make charcoal in a very smoky environment without using protective respiratory masks. He denied any mining, construction, or asbestos-related occupations. For the past year, he had been working as a dishwasher in a restaurant. On physical examination, he appeared healthy with normal vital signs and an oxygen saturation of 97%. The examination was normal except for bilateral forced expiratory wheezes. There were no signs of pulmonary hypertension, right heart failure, or clubbing. Routine laboratory tests, including a complete blood count and blood chemistry panel, were normal. Three sputum samples for mycobacteria showed no growth at 56 days. Serologies for fungal diseases were negative. Thoracic high-resolution computed axial tomography (HRCT) was performed using a 7 mm helical technique after intravenous contrast administration, followed by high-resolution imaging with 1 mm collimation every 1 cm from lung apex to base. Pulmonary function test results were: forced vital capacity (FVC) 3.46 L (91%), forced expiratory volume in 1 sec (FEV1) 2.31 L (74%), FEV1:FVC ratio 67, total lung capacity 5.27 L (95%), residual volume 1.57 L (91%), diffusion capacity for carbon monoxide 23.1 mL/mmHg/min (81%), and diffusion capacity for CO corrected for total lung capacity by single breath 4.61 mL/mmHg/L (87%). Arterial blood gases were normal.

Bronchoscopy demonstrated a large black and gray plaque in the left mainstem bronchus and multiple smaller gray and black deposits in the left upper lobe, left lower lobe, and right lower lobe. Transbronchial biopsies were obtained.

cases.case_text:
In September 2003, a 41-year-old male experienced progressive weight gain, facial redness, tremors, sweating, newly-diagnosed high blood pressure, low potassium levels, and diabetes mellitus. Physical examination showed a blood pressure of 170/110 mm Hg, a pulse rate of 88 bpm, thyroid enlargement, and features such as striae, a rounded face, central obesity, and a fat deposit on the upper back. Laboratory results indicated hyperthyroidism with undetectable TSH, free T4 at 32 pmol/L (normal: 12–22), and free T3 at 9 pmol/L (normal: 3.95–6.80). The 24-hour urinary free cortisol was elevated at 7579 nmol per day (normal range: 22–212). Thyroid ultrasound identified a multinodular goiter, and a Tc-99m-pertechnetate thyroid scan showed increased uptake in a specific area of the left thyroid gland corresponding to an autonomous adenoma. Serum calcitonin levels were normal. Basal serum cortisol and plasma ACTH levels were elevated at 1307 nmol/l (normal range: 187–724) and 22.51 pmol/l (1.98–11.4), respectively. Following a 2-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test, serum cortisol remained high at 1132 nmol/l (normal, < 80). Midnight cortisol was also elevated at 847 nmol/l. After an overnight 8-mg dexamethasone suppression test, serum cortisol decreased by 38% of basal values. CRH stimulation resulted in less than 4% increase in serum cortisol and plasma ACTH from basal values. Inferior petrosal sinus sampling did not show significant central-to-peripheral ACTH gradients.

Computed tomography (CT) scans at first presentation did not show pulmonary and/or abdominal tumors, however, both adrenals appeared enlarged with the left gland showing a tumor of 1 cm size. A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan of the head demonstrated a small 3 mm hypointense and hypoenhancing lesion of the neurohypophysis. An 111In-pentetreotide scan showed radiotracer enrichment in the left thyroid gland consistent with the region of the autonomous adenoma and faint focal octreotide enhancement in the abdomen. Positron emission tomography (PET) with 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) and colonoscopy showed normal results. An octreoscan revealed tracer accumulation in projection of the upper and middle part of the right abdomen. Additional 18F-FDG PET showed increased glucose metabolism of this abdominal area. In accordance with these findings, a 21 × 15 mm tumor mass was demonstrated on CT and MRI scans in this region. In retrospect, this tumor could also be seen in earlier CT scans but had been interpreted as normal intestine because of smaller size and only moderate uptake on octreotide scans.

A 32-year-old man presented to the Department of Periodontology at Tehran University of Medical Sciences with gingival hyperplasia around the lateral and canine teeth of the maxilla on both sides. His medical history was unremarkable. Clinical examination revealed clear vesicular lesions on the attached and marginal gingiva in the canine area, which were asymptomatic. The patient reported no previous dental issues in these areas, and the lesions had gradually appeared over the past two years. No additional lesions or alterations were detected through radiographic and clinical evaluations. Excisional biopsies were performed on both lesions, and the specimens were sent to the Department of Oral Pathology at Tehran University of Medical Sciences.

Microscopic evaluation revealed gingival tissue covered by parakeratinized squamous epithelium. Deep to the epithelium multiple dilated lymph vessels with different sizes were observed in a little loose fibrovascular tissue. These spaces were lined by a single layer of endothelial cells with flattened nuclei, and contained lymph with a few lymphocytes. Vessels just beneath the surface epithelium filled the connective tissue papilla. Both sides had similar appearance in histologic examination.

A 27-year-old nulliparous Caucasian female presented to the Gynaecology Unit with a 7-month history of pelvic pain and absence of menstruation. She also reported stress incontinence, chronic constipation, and recurrent intestinal and urinary infections. Her medical history included several congenital malformations, many of which required surgical intervention. Neonatally, she underwent anoplasty for an anorectal malformation with a rectovestibular fistula. At two months old, a laparotomy revealed hydronephrosis due to obstruction of the ectopic right ureteral orifice, leading to megadolichoureter and recurrent urinary infections. A cutaneous ureterostomy was performed to improve renal function. Two months later, another laparotomy was performed following urography that showed decreased renal function, resulting in a right nephrectomy. Histological findings indicated chronic pyelonephritis. Additional conditions included right hand thumb torsion of the metacarpal-phalangeal joint with hypotrophy of the thenar eminence, valgus, and hemisacrum (type IV sacral malformation), and bladder dysfunction treated with medication. A standard karyotype on peripheral blood cells showed a normal female karyotype (46 XX) with no chromosomal abnormalities. An ultrasound in our department revealed a complex mass originating from the right pelvis extending to the right hypochondrium and epigastrium, with a transverse extension of over 20 cm. Fluid was observed in the Douglas pouch. Abdominal and pelvic CT confirmed an irregular polylobate complex mass measuring 24 × 19.5 × 13.5 cm; the uterus and adnexa were not identified. Chest X-ray and CT scans were negative for pleural effusion or lung metastasis.

Histological examination of the pelvic mass exhibited multiple smooth muscle-like nodules with low cellularity, no cytological atypia and few mitoses. Immunohistochemical evaluation was strongly positive for desmin and actin, oestrogen receptor (ER) and progesterone receptor (PR), but negative for cytokeratin and EMA (Epithelial Membrane Antigen). Cytological examination of the peritoneal liquid revealed only reactive mesothelial cells and foamy histiocytes.

A 45-year-old Nepalese woman reported experiencing acute pain and reduced vision in both eyes for the past two months. She had been treated with oral acetazolamide and 4% pilocarpine drops, and had undergone laser iridotomy in the left eye. There was no prior history of similar episodes. Upon examination, both eyes had light perception vision, with intraocular pressure (IOP) measured at 50 mmHg in the right eye and 54 mmHg in the left eye. The left eye exhibited a mid-peripheral patent laser iridotomy. The anterior chambers were nearly flat, with diffuse pigmentation observed on the posterior corneal and anterior lens surfaces. Both eyes displayed signs of acute angle closure, including iris atrophy, glaucomflecken, prominent iris vessels, and closed angles on indentation gonioscopy. Retinoscopy was attempted but was unsuccessful due to poor fundal glow caused by diffuse pigmentation on the posterior corneal surface. The axial length was measured at 21.63 mm in the right eye and 22.52 mm in the left eye.

Ultrasound Biomicroscopy (UBM) showed an anteriorly displaced crystalline lens with extensive irido-lenticular contact and peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS) closing the angles completely in both eyes. B-Scan ultrasonography showed normal posterior segments in both eyes.

A 17-year-old female with no prior medical history was brought to the emergency room due to worsening general condition, fever, difficulty breathing, and severe intermittent coughing. Two weeks earlier, she had experienced acute pharyngitis and was treated with amoxicillin for 8 days. Upon admission, she exhibited ongoing lateral neck pain, elevated white blood cell count (13,300/m-3 with 90% neutrophils), and a C-reactive protein level of 450 mg/L. An X-ray revealed a shadow in the lower left lung. Blood samples were taken, and she was treated with amoxicillin/clavulanic acid and erythromycin.

After 48 hours in hospital, the blood cultures were positive for anaerobic Gram negative bacilli. Following the appearance of pain in the two hypochondria, a thoraco-abdominal CT scan was performed, which revealed a voluminous build-up of air and fluid in the left thorax and a heterogeneous hepato-splenomegaly.

A 12-year-old female patient presented with symptoms consistent with acute appendicitis lasting one day. Physical examination showed tenderness and rebound tenderness localized to the McBurney's point. Routine blood tests and biochemical investigations were normal except for an elevated total leukocyte count of 16,000/ml. The patient underwent an emergency appendectomy. The surgery was uneventful, with the appendix appearing swollen and inflamed. She was discharged the following day. During an outpatient follow-up, a wound infection was identified and managed conservatively. The patient later developed an incisional hernia at the site of the appendectomy, which was subsequently repaired in an elective procedure.

Histopathology analysis of the appendectomy specimen revealed the presence of caseating granulomas and Langhan's giant cells.

A 61-year-old male reported experiencing a painful mass over the lower left scapula for four months. Over the past three weeks, the pain intensified and was associated with restricted movement of the left glenohumeral joint. Physical examination identified a subcutaneous, tender, uniformly firm mass in the lower left scapular area, measuring 4.5 × 4.5 cm. There were no indications of superficial skin inflammation. The patient had no prior history of melanoma or other skin tumors.

Radiological examination showed an osteolytic lesion in the lower left scapula while bone scanning was positive with increased uptake in the same area. CT scans and MRI images of the thorax and shoulder showed a soft tissue mass 45 × 45 mm localized in the lower scapular region between infraspinatus and teres minor muscles with bone invasion of the lower part of the scapula. There were no lung metastases neither axillary nor mediastinal lymph nodes. The open biopsy specimen consisted of a rubbery, homogenous, white tissue with no attachment to the skin, implying deep location of the tumor. There were compact nests and fascicles with large rounded and spindle-shaped cells separated by connective tissue septa. The large rounded cells had pleomorphic nuclei and large amounts of clear cytoplasm while the spindle-shaped cells had palely staining eosinophilic cytoplasm. Mitoses were moderately numerous. There were areas of necrosis and hemorrhage and tumor spreading into the surrounding muscles and scapula. Immunohistochemical stains were performed with negative staining for CD68, actin and desmin antigens and with positive staining for tumor markers S-100 protein, HMB-45, NSE, EMA, cytokeratins and myosin. Histochemical stains for melanin presence were negative.

cases.case_text:
A 20-year-old African American female presented with a history of a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL) on Pap smear. A colposcopy was performed, resulting in three cervical biopsies and an endocervical curettage. All samples showed no significant pathologic alteration except for one cervical biopsy that exhibited HPV-effect. During a subsequent procedure, multiple erosions of inflammation were observed overlying the cervix.

The gross LEEP specimen measured 1.3 cm in diameter and 0.4 cm in depth. The cervical mucosa was purple-tan, smooth and glistening. No demonstrable lesions were present. Microscopically, hematoxylin- and eosin-stained sections showed cervical stroma involved by scattered cellular proliferations arranged in nests with a striking peripheral palisading arrangement and microcyst formation. A stromal reaction to these nests was not present. The cells were uniform, round to oval, and had scant cytoplasm. Nuclei were hyperchromatic, showing inconspicuous nucleoli and minimal nuclear atypia. Mitotic figures were not identified. The squamous epithelium showed occasional, sporadic foci of lymphocytic infiltration not necessarily coincident to the underlying tumor nests. Definitive squamous intraepithelial lesions were not present. A stain for EMA showed strong, diffuse cellular membrane staining of the tumor cells, whereas stains for PSA and collagen IV did not highlight cells from the lesion.

A 25-year-old male presented to the emergency room with quadriparesis following a bicycle accident. He had a history of facial deformities since early childhood, which included nasal blockage, mouth breathing, mild snoring, and progressive bowing of the shins. There was no family history of similar conditions. The patient was employed and had been commuting by bicycle when he fell, landing on his face and sustaining facial bruising. He experienced immediate neck pain and weakness in all four limbs, with limited ability to lift his arms and move his legs. He was transferred to the hospital three days post-injury. Physical examination revealed symmetrical frontal and maxillary bossing, a symmetric soft tissue bulge of the hard palate, broad forearms, sausage-like fingers, and bowing of both legs with saber shins. The nasal bridge was flat and elevated due to soft tissue thickening. No café au lait spots were noted. Neurological examination showed grade 3 muscle power in the arms with significant distal hand muscle weakness and grade 2 muscle power in the legs. All deep tendon reflexes were absent, plantar reflexes were extensor, and there was a sensory level to all modalities at the groin.

MRI of the spine showed diffuse enlargement of the laminae, transverse processes and spinous processes of the entire spine (mainly involving the posterior elements) with cervical canal stenosis and a cervical cord contusion at C 4–5 level. On T1 weighted images the posterior elements were hyperintense. The facet joints of the cervical vertebrae were also enlarged. Skull X-rays and CT scans with bone windows showed diffuse thickening of the inner and outer tables of all the skull bones with a widened diploe. The brain parenchyma, subarachnoid cisterns and paranasal sinuses were normal.

A 32-year-old woman, in her first pregnancy, was regularly seen at our antenatal outpatient clinic. Her medical history included cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN II) treated by loop excision two years prior and a bilateral breast reduction with complicated but spontaneous wound healing 13 years earlier. At 18 weeks of gestation, she was noted to have chronic hypertension with a maximum diastolic blood pressure of 95 mm Hg. At 31 weeks and 4 days, she presented with lower abdominal pain and fever. Two weeks earlier, she had experienced flu-like symptoms, headache, and a sore throat. Physical examination revealed a body temperature of 38.3°C, uterine contractions, and a fundal height corresponding to 29 weeks of gestation. The cervix was 1 cm dilated and completely effaced, with intact amniotic membranes. Ultrasound showed fetal growth at the fifth percentile and oligohydramnios. Fetal cardiotocogram (CTG) indicated a variable fetal heart rate of 160 beats per minute with late decelerations. External tocodynamometry recorded uterine contractions. Blood tests showed a high white blood cell count (WBC) of 24.4 × 10^9/L with neutrophilia and an elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) of 170 mg/L. Intravenous amoxicillin clavulanate and ritodrine were administered after a vaginal culture was taken. The contractions decreased, but fetal heart rate decelerations persisted. A caesarean section was performed, resulting in the birth of a healthy boy weighing 1227 grams (5th–10th percentile) with 1 and 5-minute Apgar scores of 9 and 10, respectively. Postoperatively, the woman continued on amoxicillin clavulanate, her temperature normalized, and CRP dropped to 84 mg/L. On day 5 postpartum, she developed a spiking fever. Physical examination of the lungs, breasts, and wound did not indicate infection. CRP rose to 321 mg/L and WBC was 27.5 × 10^9/L. Cultures from the vagina, throat, urine, and stool were negative. Serologic tests for toxoplasmosis, syphilis, rubella, cytomegalovirus, and herpes simplex virus were negative. By day 8 postpartum, she still had a spiking fever and elevated CRP despite amoxicillin clavulanate. Abdominal ultrasound and chest X-ray were normal. Amoxicillin clavulanate was discontinued. Nine days after delivery, the Pfannenstiel wound developed purulent discharge and small peri-incisional erythema; the wound borders were closed. On day 11 postpartum, a wound culture indicated staphylococcus aureus, and flucloxacillin was started. The definitive culture was negative, and flucloxacillin was switched to oral clindamycin on day 17 postpartum. The wound became more erythematous, with blue-red colored margins, infiltration, and gaping at the corners. CRP was 85 mg/L and WBC 17.7 × 10^9/L. Standard conservative wound care was recommended, and the woman was discharged to home care 19 days after delivery. Twenty-three days after the caesarean section, she was readmitted due to severe wound pain. CRP was 409 mg/L and WBC 34.1 × 10^9/L. The wound borders had a violaceous color and the ulcerative defect was progressively expanding.

Histopathologic findings of the wound biopsy showed necrosis of the epidermis with edema and bulla and an intense infiltration of granulocytes in the dermis. There were no signs of vasculitis and immunofluorescence assay was negative for immune complex vasculitis.

The patient is a 70-year-old white female with a history of right breast cancer treated approximately twelve years ago. Treatment included a lumpectomy in the upper central portion of the right breast, right axillary lymph node dissection, and postoperative radiation therapy. The cancer was characterized as pT1c, pN0, M0, estrogen receptor positive, and progesterone receptor positive invasive ductal carcinoma. She was on tamoxifen for five years following treatment. During a routine annual follow-up, she reported a new pea-sized palpable event in the inferolateral aspect of her right breast, present for one week. Clinical breast examination revealed a well-healed periareolar, curvilinear scar along the superior aspect of the right breast from the 10 o'clock to 2 o'clock axis, with no palpable events in this region. However, a less than one centimeter palpable nodule was noted in the mid to peripheral portion of the lower outer quadrant of the right breast at the 7 o'clock axis, appearing relatively superficial within the breast tissue.

Mammography showed stable, asymmetrical, increased density to the tissue within the upper retroareolar portion of her right breast, consistent with her prior lumpectomy site. However, a new 0.8 × 0.5 cm mammographic density was noted in the inferolateral portion of her right breast. Targeted right breast ultrasound showed a 0.78 × 0.63 × 0.49 cm hypoechoic lesion that was located in the 7 o'clock axis and approximately 4 cm from the nipple, which was associated with acoustic shadowing. A minimally invasive right breast ultrasound-guided 8 gauge Mammotome® vacuum-assisted biopsy was performed. Microscopic evaluation revealed fragments of breast parenchyma in which a bland spindle cell proliferation was present, forming long interlacing fascicles. The cells showed cigar-shaped nuclei with vesicular chromatin and pinpoint nucleoli that were dispersed amidst varying degrees of collagen deposition, ranging from scant to thick bundles. In some fragments, the proliferation could be seen entrapping lobular units. Immunohistochemical stains for cytokeratin were negative.

A 75-year-old Caucasian female, who does not smoke, presented for a gastroenterology evaluation due to rectal bleeding. She has mild essential hypertension, which is well controlled with diltiazem, and intermittently uses oral aspirin, 81 mg per day. In 1966, she underwent a total abdominal hysterectomy, during which both ovaries were removed. At the time of evaluation, she occasionally used supplemental estrogen but was uncertain about the start date. Her only other surgery was an uncomplicated laparoscopic cholecystectomy in 1996. The patient's BMI was 26. Vital signs and physical examination were normal, except for a heme-positive stool. An abdominal CT scan showed no significant abnormalities, but a pelvic CT scan revealed a 7 cm partially calcified mass at the upper pelvic inlet, indistinguishable from the bowel.

Ultrasound of this lesion confirmed a 74 × 45 × 49 mm heterogeneous (partially echogenic) mass in the upper right pelvis. The specimen demonstrated positive vimentin staining for mesenchymal spindle and round cells, consistent with benign ovarian stromal neoplasm.

A 24-year-old female presented with a thumb-sized subcutaneous mass on the right side of the pubic region, persisting for two years. She reported an increase in both the size of the mass and associated pain, prompting her to seek medical attention. She had no history of pregnancy or dysmenorrhea. Physical examination revealed a 2 × 3 cm subcutaneous mass located just above the right edge of the pubic tubercle, characterized by a slightly rough surface, unclear borders, and mild tenderness. The mass showed no adhesion to the skin and only slight adhesion to the subcutaneous fat tissue, but was firmly attached to the underlying structures without mobility. The overlying skin appeared normal. Laboratory tests indicated no signs of inflammation with WBC at 6400/μl and CRP at 0.1, and slight anemia with Hb at 11.8 g/dl. Pelvic CT imaging identified an irregular subcutaneous mass just above the right edge of the pubic tubercle, with an X-ray absorbance density similar to that of muscle. During surgery, the mass was accessed via an incision on the medial side of the right groin region. It was manually separated from the subcutaneous fat tissue but was firmly attached to the uterine round ligament with a poorly defined border. The mass was excised along with a portion of the uterine round ligament. No inguinal hernia or sac was observed. Macroscopically, the tumor had fat tissue on its surface, and the cross-section showed a whitish-yellow color with an irregular round shape and indistinct boundaries adhering to the surrounding fat tissue. Small spots containing brownish mucus were noted.

The H&E staining of the removed tissue showed several small hollow glands scattered inside the tumor with a stromal structure. The hollow glands were lined with columnar epithelial layers and surrounded by proliferated stromal cells. Immunohistochemical analyses revealed that antibodies against CA125, estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, CD10, and COX-2 stained positively, but no staining of the CA19-9 antibody was observed. The CA125 antibody stained weakly, mainly in the inner and outer surfaces of the cytoplasm in the glandular endothelial cells, without staining the nuclei of the endothelial and stromal cells. The estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and COX-2 antibodies stained both in the stromal and endothelial cells. However, estrogen and progesterone receptor antibodies stained positively only in the nucleus and not the cytoplasm. The estrogen receptor antibody stained more positively in the endothelial cells than in the stromal cells, while the progesterone receptor antibody stained strongly and more positively in the stromal cells than in that of the endothelial cells. COX-2 had stained stronger in the cytoplasm and the nuclei of the endothelial cells than in that of the stromal cells. CD10 stained strongly positive in only the cytoplasm of the stromal cells.

A 65-year-old woman, who does not smoke, presented with a 6-month history of persistent dry cough. Imaging studies identified a solitary nodule in the right upper lung field. The patient also reported mild, persistent lumbar pain over the past two years, for which she had been taking nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Physical examination revealed a barely palpable mass in the lumbar area, while reflexes in the lower extremities were normal. Laboratory tests showed no abnormalities, and tumor markers were within normal ranges. MRI and CT scans identified an ill-defined osteolytic lesion in the L5 vertebra, featuring splotch calcification, cortical permeation, and extension into surrounding soft tissues. A chest CT scan showed the lung nodule to have similar characteristics. An attempt to biopsy the lung nodule was made, but the sample was insufficient for further analysis. Due to the risk of collapse of the L5 vertebra, the patient underwent spinal surgery, and the mass was excised.

The histopathological examination revealed a moderately cellular multilobular neoplasm with chondroid and myxoid matrix and focal necrosis. Under high power view, multicellular lacunae of chondrocytes with moderate nuclear pleomorphism and hypercromasia were observed. Mitotic figures were numerous. On immunohistochemical examination > 25 % of the neoplastic cells exhibited nuclear immunoreactivity for the tumor suppressor protein p53. Furthermore < 1 % of the neoplastic cells were in cell cycle, as estimated with the immunohistochemical marker MIB-1 (ki-67).

A 48-year-old male presented with blood in the urine and a dull, aching pain in the right side of the lower back. General examination did not reveal any abnormalities, with no swollen lymph nodes or bone tenderness. The chest, cardiovascular, and neurological examinations were normal. Abdominal examination identified a mildly tender mass in the right lumbar region. Routine laboratory tests, including a complete blood count, chest X-ray, and renal function tests, were normal. Urine analysis showed a significant number of red blood cells under high power field.

An ultrasound examination of the abdomen revealed an echogenic mass in the upper part of the right kidney measuring 11 × 10 cm. No calcified areas were noted; the renal pelvis and renal vein were not involved. The other abdominal viscera were radiologically normal. There was no lymph node enlargement. Microscopically, the tumor was highly cellular comprising of epithelial, blastemic and stromal elements. The epithelial element comprised of tubules admixed with blastemic cells. The tubular lining cells had elongated, molded, and wedge shaped nuclei exhibiting frequent mitoses. The tubular pattern resembled pseudo-rosettes at places. The blastemic component had solid areas showing cells with oval nuclei and scanty cytoplasm. The stroma with spindle cells had no specific differentiation. There was no area showing anaplasia.

A 24-year-old Tunisian woman was admitted to the hospital 2 weeks after vaginal delivery with a 10-day history of pain in the right leg, right iliac fossa, and flank. These symptoms worsened over the following days. The patient developed chest pain, tachycardia, dyspnea, and fever, which increased in severity. She did not respond to antibiotic therapy. Her past medical history included recurrent oral and genital aphthous, pseudofolliculitis, and erythema nodosum in the lower extremities. She had previously been on colchicine therapy but had discontinued it on her own. Physical examination upon admission revealed a fever of 38.5°C, oral ulcers on the lips, hypopigmented genital scars, and pseudofolliculitis. Heart sounds and bilateral lung areas were normal upon auscultation. Laboratory tests indicated an inflammatory condition with a high erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 130 mm in the first hour, a C reactive protein level of 78.3 mg/dl (normal range 0–5 mg/dl), a hemoglobin value of 11 g/dl, and a leukocyte count of 5400/mm3 with a normal differential count. Urinalysis, liver and kidney function tests were normal; antinuclear antibody tests were negative; platelet count, protein C, protein S, and antithrombin III levels were within normal limits; and anticardiolipin antibodies and lupus anticoagulant were absent. Her plasma total homocysteine level was 17 μmol/l (normal < 10 μmol/l). Chest radiography and electrocardiogram were normal except for sinus tachycardia.

Color Doppler echography and abdominal computed tomographic scan (CT) revealed an ascending thrombosis of the iliac and right ovarian veins. Chest helical CT revealed a bilateral mural thrombus of segmental pulmonary arteries and a triangular area of opacity representing a pulmonary infarct at the posterior segment of the right lower lobe.

A 70-year-old male patient was referred for coronary revascularization due to angina (Canadian Cardiovascular Society class 2) and three vessel disease, with good left ventricular function. He had no significant past medical history and his physical examination was unremarkable. Preoperative risk assessment scores were: EuroSCORE standard 3 (age), logistic 1.82. Preoperative investigations showed a white cell count (WCC) of 15.6 × 10^9/L (neutrophils 10.1 × 10^9/L, monocytes 2.5 × 10^9/L) and urinalysis positive for blood. Despite denying any urinary or respiratory symptoms, he was treated empirically for a lower urinary tract infection and discharged home. Urine culture was negative. Two weeks later, the WCC remained elevated at 14.2 × 10^9/L (neutrophils 10.5 × 10^9/L, monocytes 1.6 × 10^9/L), although he remained asymptomatic and was eager to proceed. Coronary artery bypass grafting was performed using the left internal mammary artery and saphenous vein grafts. Cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) time was 76 minutes with aortic cross-clamp for 39 minutes, using antegrade cold crystalloid cardioplegia. The patient came off CPB easily and remained haemodynamically stable thereafter. He was extubated quickly and returned to the ward on the first postoperative day. Routine blood tests showed a leukocytosis (46.9 × 10^9/L) with marked neutrophilia (38.5 × 10^9/L) and monocytosis (8.4 × 10^9/L). Late on the first postoperative day, his condition worsened with progressive hypoxia, oliguria, and metabolic acidosis. He was readmitted to the intensive care unit for non-invasive ventilation and inotropic support. On the morning of the second postoperative day, he remained hypoxic and oliguric. A pulmonary artery catheter indicated low cardiac output state and low systemic vascular resistance. He was reintubated and mechanically ventilated, inotropic therapy was increased, and continuous veno-venous haemofiltration and broad-spectrum antibiotics were started. A cardiac origin of low cardiac output was excluded, and sepsis or splanchnic ischemia were considered as potential causes of his systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) and multi-organ dysfunction (MOD).

Computed tomography of the thorax and abdomen showed bilateral ground glass shadowing of the lung parenchyma consistent with acute respiratory distress syndrome.

A 7-month-old female infant from a Sudanese western tribe was referred with concerns of malnutrition. Upon examination, the patient exhibited confluent, arched, and well-defined eyebrows, long curly eyelashes, low front and back hairlines, an upturned nose, down-turned corners of the mouth, thin lips, a long philtrum, a small lower jaw, and a protruding upper jaw. Additional findings included microcephaly, excessive body hair, a short neck, small broad hands with a simian crease, proximal insertion of the thumb, and clinodactyly of the fifth finger. The patient had a low-pitched cry, a short neck with limited movement, stiff muscle tone (unable to sit, still fisting), fixed flexion of both elbows, and no signs of speaking or babbling. Other observations included a tied tongue and thin skin. The patient's length was approximately 27 inches, weight was 3 kilograms, and skull circumference was 35 cm. An X-ray revealed crowded ribs with short distances between each rib. Peripheral blood was cultured in RPMI 1640 medium for 72 hours, followed by metaphase arrest using Colcemide. Cells were harvested, treated with a hypotonic solution, and fixed with methanol and acetic acid. The cells were then dropped on clean slides and stained with Wright's stain for chromosome banding. Clonality criteria and karyotypic descriptions followed ISCN recommendations.

X-ray showed delayed bone development. Her brain stem evoked potential test showed conductive hearing loss. Hepatomegally was shown by ultrasonography. Analysis of 11 metaphase cells showed 46, XX in all cells.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

In August 2003, a 20-year-old woman, 16 weeks pregnant and mother of one, visited the orthopaedic outpatient clinic due to a 2-month history of a slowly enlarging, painless mass in the right hypothenar eminence. She is right-hand dominant and a housewife. There was no history of trauma, insect bites, or drainage from the area. Her past medical and surgical history was unremarkable, and she was not on any prescribed medication. There was no family history of tumors, and she denied smoking, alcohol, and drug abuse. Physical examination revealed a non-tender, firm, well-demarcated mass tethered to the subcutaneous tissues, surrounded by mild erythema, measuring approximately 2.5 cm × 3.0 cm. No palpable lymph nodes were found at the ipsilateral elbow or axilla, and no other abnormal signs were noted. Haematological and biochemical investigations were within normal limits. A plain X-ray of the right hand and forearm showed no abnormalities. Magnetic resonance imaging indicated that the mass infiltrated all skin layers and encircled the ulnar artery without affecting the underlying bones. The absence of a signal void within the mass ruled out certain vascular conditions. Ultrasound-guided needle biopsy revealed areas consistent with collagenous fibrous tissue of varying cellularity, with minimal mitotic activity.
